p: 'As long as you can,' McGilvery said, and rode away.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Bigelow's Last Stand”, paragraph 5 of 10

p: Bigelow ordered his battery to hook their guns to prolonges — long ropes that allowed artillerymen to move the guns while still firing — and begin a fighting withdrawal through the Trostle Farm lane.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Bigelow's Last Stand”, paragraph 6 of 10

p: What followed was one of the most desperate artillery actions of the war. The 9th Massachusetts fired as they retreated, horses falling, men dropping at the guns. Bigelow was wounded. The battery lost one gun stuck in a stone wall as Confederate infantry closed in from three sides. The last section fired canister into advancing Mississippians from a range of fifty yards.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Bigelow's Last Stand”, paragraph 7 of 10

p: Bigelow lost 28 men and one gun. He bought McGilvery the twenty minutes he needed.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Bigelow's Last Stand”, paragraph 8 of 10

p: When Confederate infantry finally overran the Trostle Farm, they found it abandoned. McGilvery's Plum Run Line was formed and waiting.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Bigelow's Last Stand”, paragraph 9 of 10

p: The cannonball hole in the Trostle Farm barn wall — a Confederate artillery round that missed Bigelow's withdrawing battery — is still visible today. It is one of the most photographed details on the Gettysburg battlefield.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Bigelow's Last Stand”, paragraph 10 of 10

p: Winfield Scott Hancock had been riding hard along Cemetery Ridge for twenty minutes, trying to hold together a line that was dissolving in front of him. The III Corps was gone — shattered, streaming back from the Peach Orchard and the Wheatfield. The gap in the Union center was real and it was widening.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The First Minnesota”, paragraph 1 of 12

p: Across the fields, Cadmus Wilcox's Alabama brigade was advancing at the double-quick toward that gap. If they reached Cemetery Ridge, the Union line would be cut in two.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The First Minnesota”, paragraph 2 of 12

p: Hancock turned in his saddle. The only regiment near at hand was the 1st Minnesota — 262 officers and men under Colonel William Colvill.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The First Minnesota”, paragraph 3 of 12

p: 'My God, are these all the men we have here?' Hancock said.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The First Minnesota”, paragraph 4 of 12

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The First Minnesota”, paragraph 5 of 12

p: Colvill understood what the order meant. He turned to his regiment: 'Forward, double-quick!'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The First Minnesota”, paragraph 6 of 12

p: The 262 men of the 1st Minnesota — a state with fewer than 200,000 people — charged into Wilcox's entire brigade.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The First Minnesota”, paragraph 7 of 12

p: The fighting was savage and brief. The regiment drove into the Confederate line with bayonets and clubbed rifles, and for a few minutes the Confederate advance actually stopped. The Alabamians had not expected this. They had not expected anything to be there at all.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The First Minnesota”, paragraph 8 of 12

p: But 262 men cannot hold long against 1,700. The 1st Minnesota was shredded. Colvill went down, shot in three places. The regimental commander, the lieutenant colonel, the major — all hit. Companies were reduced to handfuls. The regiment fell back toward Cemetery Ridge.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The First Minnesota”, paragraph 9 of 12

p: But they had bought the five minutes Hancock needed. Reinforcements arrived and closed the gap.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The First Minnesota”, paragraph 10 of 12
